cues.text: An Unusual Childhood Devotion
Born in 1991 in London to Italian parents, Carlo Acutis moved with his family to Milan while still an infant.
Though his own parents were not especially devout at the time, Carlo showed an unusual and self-directed attraction to the faith from early childhood.
He reportedly asked to attend daily Mass and pray the Rosary well before it became part of his family's regular practice—a devotion his mother later said drew her own faith deeper as well.
An Ordinary, Likeable Boy
By all accounts, Carlo was an entirely normal and well-liked teenager who enjoyed video games, cared for pets, and played soccer.
He taught himself computer programming and web design, skills unusually advanced for his age, which he increasingly turned toward explicitly religious purposes rather than purely recreational ones.
Cataloguing Eucharistic Miracles
Drawing on his technical skill and deep personal devotion to the Eucharist, Carlo spent roughly the last two and a half years of his life researching and building a comprehensive website.

He once said, "The Eucharist is the highway to heaven" It documented Church-recognized Eucharistic miracles from around the world, eventually cataloguing over 150 cases by country and date, complete with maps and images.
He organized the material into a portable exhibition still displayed in parishes worldwide.
Quiet Generosity
Alongside his technical project, Carlo was known for simple, consistent acts of charity: giving away his allowance to help the poor.
He stood up for classmates who were bullied at school, small, unremarkable kindnesses remembered by those who knew him as entirely characteristic of an otherwise ordinary teenage life.
A Sudden Illness
In October 2006, Carlo fell suddenly and severely ill with what was diagnosed as fulminant leukemia.
He died roughly a week after diagnosis, on 12 October 2006, at only fifteen years old.
In the days before his death, he offered his suffering for the pope and for the Church.
Legacy
Carlo's cause for canonization opened in 2012, and he was beatified in 2020 following the Vatican's recognition of a miraculous healing attributed to his intercession.
Canonized on 7 September 2025 by Pope Leo XIV, Carlo Acutis became the first millennial saint recognized by the Catholic Church.
He is popularly honored as an informal patron of the internet and computer programmers.
This reminds us that ordinary digital tools, turned toward genuine purposes, can become instruments of real and lasting evangelization.
